## #1585 a5 AICPU topology probe fails on driver 25.7.rc1.6 (CPU_TOPO rc=65534), hard-failing every device run

- State: closed
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1585
- Created: 2026-07-29T10:36:54Z
- Updated: 2026-08-03T02:22:25Z
- Closed: 2026-08-03T02:22:25Z

### Body

## Background

Hit in `pypto-lib` on an A5 host after the box was upgraded to driver
**25.7.rc1.6** (2026-07-28). After the upgrade **every** A5 device run fails
during runtime init:

```
[WARN]  query_cpu_topo: halGetDeviceInfoByBuff(CPU_TOPO) rc=65534 total=0
[WARN]  query_cpu_topo: dsmi_get_device_info(CPU_TOPO)    rc=65534 total=0
[ERROR] AICPU topology probe failed; affinity gate will drop all threads
RuntimeError: run failed with code -1
```

Both CPU_TOPO entry points in `probe_aicpu_topology` return `rc=65534` on this
driver, and `src/a5/platform/onboard/host/device_runner.cpp:225` hard-returns
`-1` when the probe fails and `n_sched > 0`. The result is that no a5 kernel can
run at all — this is a hard blocker, not a degradation.

We are running with a **local patch** to get unblocked (below) and would like it
reviewed / replaced with a proper fix.

### Environment

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| simpler | `8e00319e` (also reproduces at `9922afdb`, the commit pypto pins) |
| pypto | `a8ef572f` |
| pypto-lib | `4c346f0` |
| ptoas | v0.48 |
| pto-isa | `83d01313` |
| **driver** | **25.7.rc1.6** |
| CANN | 9.1.0-beta.3 |
| host | x86_64, Ascend 950 (A5) |

## What we established

- **It is not the command number.** `probe` hardcodes
  `DSMI_MAIN_CMD_SOC_INFO = 14`, and that enum value is still 14 in this
  driver's `dsmi_common_interface.h`.
- **`halGetDeviceInfo` itself works.** `query_occupy` (AICPU / OCCUPY) succeeds —
  execution reaches the CPU_TOPO warn, which only happens after OCCUPY returns
  cleanly. So it is specifically the CPU_TOPO query that this driver rejects.
- **Both entry points fail**, `halGetDeviceInfoByBuff` and
  `dsmi_get_device_info`, with the same `rc=65534`.
- **Rolling simpler back does not help.** `aicpu_topology_probe.cpp` is
  byte-identical (sha1 `17298ba92b9a`) at `9922afdb`, `723bb143` and `main`
  `8e00319e`; it first appeared in `96fb746c` (#963) together with the hard
  fail, 378 commits back. So no simpler version in pypto's compatible range
  avoids it.
- The existing comment in the file notes `rc=65534` is what the driver returns
  when its internal size check on the struct layout fails — consistent with the
  `DsmiCpuTopo` layout having been verified against an older driver header.

## Our local patch (for reference, not a proposed fix)

`query_occupy` still works, and OCCUPY alone gives the **cpu_ids** — which is the
only field the on-device filter gate actually matches against (it compares
`sched_getcpu()` to `ALLOWED_CPUS[]`). The topology fields only feed
`compute_allowed_cpus`' placement policy. So when CPU_TOPO is unavailable we fall
back to building the pool from the OCCUPY bitmap, assuming one thread per phy:

```diff
diff --git a/src/a5/platform/onboard/host/aicpu_topology_probe.cpp b/src/a5/platform/onboard/host/aicpu_topology_probe.cpp
index b2f4e22a..aaabc1a1 100644
--- a/src/a5/platform/onboard/host/aicpu_topology_probe.cpp
+++ b/src/a5/platform/onboard/host/aicpu_topology_probe.cpp
@@ -144,7 +144,37 @@ bool probe_aicpu_topology_uncached(uint32_t device_id, std::vector<AicpuLogicalC
     if (!query_occupy(device_id, occupy)) return false;
 
     DsmiCpuTopo topo{};
-    if (!query_cpu_topo(device_id, topo)) return false;
+    if (!query_cpu_topo(device_id, topo)) {
+        // LOCAL DIAGNOSTIC PATCH -- not for commit.
+        //
+        // Driver 25.7.rc1.6 rejects both CPU_TOPO entry points (dsmi returns
+        // rc=65534), which otherwise hard-fails every a5 device run in
+        // device_runner.cpp. OCCUPY still works, and OCCUPY alone gives the
+        // cpu_ids -- which is the only field the on-device filter gate
+        // actually matches against (it compares sched_getcpu() to
+        // ALLOWED_CPUS[]). The topology fields feed compute_allowed_cpus'
+        // placement policy only, so losing them costs SMT/cluster packing
+        // quality, not correctness.
+        //
+        // Assume one thread per phy (no SMT info available). If the SKU really
+        // is SMT, two siblings may get packed together -> slower, still valid.
+        LOG_WARN(
+            "aicpu_topology_probe: CPU_TOPO unavailable; falling back to OCCUPY-only pool "
+            "(degraded placement, no SMT/cluster awareness)"
+        );
+        for (int32_t i = 0; i < 64; ++i) {
+            if (((occupy >> i) & 1ULL) == 0) continue;
+            AicpuLogicalCpu e{};
+            e.cpu_id = i;
+            e.phy_cpu_id = i;
+            e.hyperthread_id = 0;
+            e.cluster_id = e.phy_cpu_id / 2;
+            e.die_id = e.phy_cpu_id / 4;
+            out_user_cpus.push_back(e);  // ascending by construction
+        }
+        LOG_WARN("aicpu_topology_probe: OCCUPY-only pool has %zu cpu_ids", out_user_cpus.size());
+        return !out_user_cpus.empty();
+    }
 
     for (uint32_t i = 0; i < topo.total_nums; ++i) {
         const DsmiSingleCpu &c = topo.cpus[i];
```

On this host that yields a 5-cpu pool and **restores all a5 device execution**;
the full DeepSeek-V4-Pro single-card suite then runs (26/27 passing, the
remainder unrelated to this).

The cost is placement quality, not correctness: without `phy_cpu_id` /
`hyperthread_id` the sched/orch packing can no longer avoid SMT siblings or pick
the best cluster. That is why we are not proposing it as the fix — it is a
unblock-the-host workaround.

## Ask

1. Is driver 25.7.rc1.6 expected to support the CPU_TOPO query, i.e. is the
   `DsmiCpuTopo` layout stale against this driver's header? (There is no
   `cpu_topo` struct in the shipped `dsmi_common_interface.h` to verify against.)
2. Independent of that — should a failed topology probe really be fatal? A
   documented degraded path (e.g. the OCCUPY-only pool above, or the basic
   non-filter gate that the sim platforms already use) would keep hosts running
   when a driver stops answering this query.

Happy to test any patch on this host.

## #1604 [Code Health] Scene tests hold an NPU lock through their CPU phases, and recompile every kernel on every CI run

- State: open
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1604
- Created: 2026-07-31T00:53:16Z
- Updated: 2026-08-06T09:11:41Z
- Closed: 

### Body

### Category

Technical Debt (cleanup, refactor)

### Component

Tests

### Description

Two related inefficiencies in how scene tests consume devices. Both were quantified while investigating why `qwen3_14b_decode` needed to be excluded from the a2a3 sweep (fixed in #1601); the numbers below are measurements, not estimates.

**a) Kernel compilation has no cross-run cache.**

`_compile_cache` is a module-level dict cleared at session end, so a callable is compiled once per pytest session and never reused across CI runs. Every run recompiles every kernel from source with `ccec`.

Measured for `qwen3_14b_decode` on this repo's a2a3 box — 36 incores plus one orchestration:

| | Wall |
| --- | --- |
| ordinary incore, each | 1.1–1.3 s |
| orchestration | 6.6 s |
| vendor FAI kernel, AIV variant | **8.4 s** (1330 KiB) |
| **total for this one case** | **59 s** |

The key machinery already exists — `l3_compile_cache_key()` composes a stable key from `(qualname, name, platform, runtime, pto_isa_token)`. It is only ever used against an in-memory dict. Adding a source-content hash and persisting to `build/cache/kernels/` would make this survive: `build/` is gitignored and the self-hosted runners' workspaces persist across runs, so CI would pay compilation once per kernel change instead of once per PR.

**b) The device lock is held through work that never touches the device.**

`ci.yml` wraps the whole pytest invocation in `task-submit ... --run "python -m pytest ..."`, so kernel compilation, fixture construction and golden computation all run while holding a card.

For `qwen3_14b_decode` after #1601:

| Phase | Wall | Needs a device? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| kernel compilation | 59 s | no |
| `generate_inputs` (38 GiB fixture) | 13 s | no |
| `compute_golden` (40 layers, thread-capped) | ~43 s | no |
| host→device upload, device run, comparison | remainder | yes — the device is busy for **tens of milliseconds** |

So ~115 s of card time per run, for ~36 ms of device work. This is not specific to qwen: `test_hello_worker` — `Worker(level=2).init()` then `close()`, no kernels at all — takes 4.1 s, and the eleven allreduce collectives take 17.9–20.6 s each despite exercising five different algorithms (onephase / twophase / ring / bidirectional_ring / ibing), which says the cost is fixed overhead rather than the collective.

The contention this creates is measurable on the same job (`st-onboard-a2a3`, ci run 30507320146, job 90761014912): **1187 s of 2297 s — 52% — was spent queued waiting for free dies**, across 8 separate `task-submit` acquisitions. The first one waited 976 s for four cards.

`compute_golden` already runs *before* the device run (`scene_test.py:1288`, `:1367`), so it is hoistable in principle. Compilation is the harder half, and (a) is its prerequisite: a pre-compile pass outside the lock only helps if the artifacts survive into the locked run.

### Location

- `simpler_setup/scene_test.py:39` — `_compile_cache` is an in-memory dict; `:66` clears it at session end; `:985` / `:1029` are its only read and write
- `simpler_setup/scene_test.py:54` — `l3_compile_cache_key()`, the key machinery that exists but never reaches disk
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml:504`, `:525`, `:604` — the `task-submit ... --run "pytest ..."` wrappers that put every CPU phase inside the device lock

### Proposed Fix

Two steps, in order, because the second depends on the first.

**a) Persist the compile cache.** Extend `l3_compile_cache_key()` with a hash of the kernel sources and their include closure, and back it with `build/cache/kernels/<key>`. Cross-run reuse on the self-hosted runners; GitHub-hosted sim jobs would need `actions/cache` to benefit, which can come later or not at all.

**b) Acquire the card after the CPU phases.** With (a) in place, the shape becomes: compile (and ideally build fixtures and goldens) outside `task-submit`, then take the lock only for the device run. Options worth weighing — a warm-up pass before the locked invocation, versus the harness acquiring the lock lazily at first device touch. The first is far simpler and probably enough.

Worth noting one trade-off for (b): the current 8 separate acquisitions cost ~210 s of re-queueing across the five trailing smoke steps, so there is a competing argument for holding **one** lock for the whole job. That is the opposite direction and the two need deciding together — shorter total device-seconds for the fleet, versus shorter wall time for this job.

### Priority

Medium (minor risk, should fix in next few releases)

## #1608 [Docs] Four doc directories have no index page, so their links 404 on the published site

- State: closed
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1608
- Created: 2026-07-31T02:44:09Z
- Updated: 2026-08-04T11:56:17Z
- Closed: 2026-08-04T11:56:17Z

### Body

### Documentation Location

- `docs/hardware/` (4 pages)
- `docs/troubleshooting/` (7 pages)
- `docs/remote-l3-worker-design/` (6 pages)
- `docs/troubleshooting/device-error-codes/` (4 pages)

Linked as directories from `docs/README.md` (three rows), `docs/dfx/README.md`, and `docs/user/how-to/debug-a-failed-run.md`.

### What's Wrong or Missing?

These four directories are linked with a trailing slash — `[hardware/](hardware/)` — rather than at a specific page. GitHub renders that as a directory listing, so it works when reading the repo. **MkDocs leaves the link as-is and there is no `index.html` to serve, so every one of them 404s on <https://hw-native-sys.github.io/simpler/>.**

MkDocs does report it, at `INFO`:

```
INFO - Doc file 'README.md' contains an unrecognized relative link 'hardware/', it was left as is.
INFO - Doc file 'README.md' contains an unrecognized relative link 'troubleshooting/', it was left as is.
INFO - Doc file 'README.md' contains an unrecognized relative link 'remote-l3-worker-design/', it was left as is.
INFO - Doc file 'dfx/README.md' contains an unrecognized relative link '../troubleshooting/', it was left as is.
INFO - Doc file 'user/how-to/debug-a-failed-run.md' contains an unrecognized relative link '../../troubleshooting/device-error-codes/', it was left as is.
```

`--strict` only fails on `warn` and above, so this builds clean today. The knob is `validation.links.unrecognized_links` in `mkdocs.yml`, currently at its default of `info`. It was deliberately left there in #1581 — that PR raised `validation.links.anchors` to `warn` and fixed the six broken anchors it exposed, and recorded that these five directory links are the remaining class, because fixing them means **adding index pages, not editing links**.

Twenty-one pages across the four directories are therefore reachable on the site only through `nav`, and the three that are excluded from `nav` on purpose (`remote-l3-worker-design/*`, `troubleshooting/device-error-codes/*`, `investigations/*` — see `not_in_nav`) are reachable **only** through these dead links.

### Suggested Improvement

Add a `README.md` to each of the four directories, in the shape `docs/dfx/README.md` and `docs/investigations/README.md` already use — a short statement of what the directory is for, plus a table of its pages and what each covers. Then register them in `mkdocs.yml`'s `nav` so the sidebar reaches them too.

Once all four exist, raise `validation.links.unrecognized_links` to `warn` in `mkdocs.yml` so `--strict` catches the next one. That step is the point of the exercise: without it, the same class of link rots back in silently, exactly as the anchors did before #1581.

`docs/README.md` already states the rule this would satisfy: *"New docs belong in one of the groups below, and in a subdirectory when the group already has one."* Four of the five subdirectories it names have no index of their own.

### Additional Context

Related: #1581 (raised `anchors` to `warn`, fixed the six broken anchors, and scoped these out explicitly).

Discovered while making `mkdocs build --strict` meaningful; the site is built and deployed by `.github/workflows/docs.yml` on every push to `main`.

## #1616 [Code Health] L3 comm-domain examples hand-roll a Worker and their own verification, which @scene_test already supports

- State: closed
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1616
- Created: 2026-07-31T09:42:01Z
- Updated: 2026-08-11T04:24:17Z
- Closed: 2026-08-11T04:24:17Z

### Body

### Category

Technical Debt (cleanup, refactor)

### Component

Tests

### Description

Seven example tests that allocate a communication domain are plain pytest
functions that construct a `Worker(level=3, ...)` by hand, drive it, and then
compare results with hand-written tolerance checks. They total **1391 lines**.

The reason to look at them again is that **the scene-test framework already
supports everything they do** — this was checked rather than assumed, because
the obvious guess is that comm domains are what `@scene_test` cannot express.
They are not:

| Capability the demos need | Already used by |
| ------------------------- | --------------- |
| L3 `@scene_test` class | 8 classes: 5 collectives suites + `test_l3_dependency` / `test_l3_group` / `test_l3_host_buffer_registration` |
| Python orchestration function | `CALLABLE["orchestration"]`, invoked at `simpler_setup/scene_test.py:1402` |
| `orch.allocate_domain(...)` with `CommBufferSpec` | `tests/st/worker/collectives/_helpers.py:117` and `:186`, inside `allreduce_orch_fn` — the same call shape as the demos |
| **Per-rank** goldens | `tests/st/worker/collectives/all_to_all/test_all_to_all.py:103` — `compute_golden` writes a different expected tensor per rank via `out_{r}` |
| `device_count`, `num_sub_workers`, `enable_sdma` | `CASES[*]["config"]`; `enable_sdma` since #1609 |

So the split in the tree is not between "L3 with domains" and "L3 without" — the
collectives suites are L3 *with* domains and are ordinary scene tests. The seven
demos are simply older than the framework support.

What being plain functions costs them:

- **Verification is hand-rolled.** Each file computes a max-abs-diff, ANDs it
  into a local `ok`, and `run()` returns `0`/`1` for `assert run(...) == 0`
  (3–4 such sites per file). There is no golden tensor and nothing checks that
  the comparison itself is still meaningful — a mis-edited tolerance passes
  silently, where `compute_golden` would not.
- **No case parametrization**, so `--rounds` / `--case` and multi-shape coverage
  are unavailable.
- **Device allocation is not the dispatcher's**, so these run in the Resource
  phase as standalone subprocesses rather than sharing the pooled L2/L3 Worker.
- **a2a3 and a5 copies drift independently.** The pairs differ by only 8–21
  lines (`async_notify_demo` 11, `deferred_notify_demo` 8,
  `sdma_async_completion_demo` 21), and `platforms` is a `CASES` field — so the
  duplication exists only because the hand-rolled form has nowhere to put it.

**Counter-argument, stated deliberately:** these are *examples*, and a demo that
reads top-to-bottom without framework indirection has real value for someone
learning the API. The same argument is what closed golden vectorisation in
[`docs/investigations/2026-07-qwen-scene-test-406s-decomposition.md`](../blob/main/docs/investigations/2026-07-qwen-scene-test-406s-decomposition.md)
("a reference implementation whose readability is the point"). This issue is
therefore a *decision request* as much as a cleanup: converting all seven is
mechanical, but whether examples should read like `tests/st/` is a judgement the
maintainers should make before anyone starts.

### Location

The seven files, all under `examples/`:

```text
a2a3/tensormap_and_ringbuffer/async_notify_demo/test_async_notify_demo.py           179
a2a3/tensormap_and_ringbuffer/deferred_notify_demo/test_deferred_notify_demo.py     191
a2a3/tensormap_and_ringbuffer/sdma_async_completion_demo/test_*.py                  209
a5/tensormap_and_ringbuffer/async_notify_demo/test_async_notify_demo.py             176
a5/tensormap_and_ringbuffer/deferred_notify_demo/test_deferred_notify_demo.py       191
a5/tensormap_and_ringbuffer/sdma_async_completion_demo/test_*.py                    212
a5/tensormap_and_ringbuffer/urma_deferred_completion_demo/test_*.py                 233
```

Hand-rolled Worker, e.g.
`examples/a2a3/tensormap_and_ringbuffer/sdma_async_completion_demo/test_sdma_async_completion_demo.py:128`.

The template to follow: `tests/st/worker/collectives/` — `_helpers.py` (265
lines, shared orch functions) plus thin per-case classes (`all_to_all` is 131
lines and covers several rank counts).

Two `tests/ut/py/test_worker/` files also use `allocate_domain`
(`test_dynamic_alloc_hw.py`, `test_dynamic_alloc_sim.py`). Those are unit tests
and are **out of scope** — they should stay plain functions.

### Proposed Fix

If the decision is to convert, the shape is already proven by the collectives
suites:

1. Factor each demo's `orch_fn` into a shared helper module, as
   `tests/st/worker/collectives/_helpers.py` does.
2. Replace each `run()` with a `@scene_test(level=3, runtime=...)` class whose
   `CASES` carry `device_count` / `num_sub_workers` / `enable_sdma` and whose
   `platforms` list absorbs the a2a3-vs-a5 split, collapsing the near-duplicate
   pairs.
3. Turn each hand-rolled tolerance check into `compute_golden`, per-rank via the
   `out_{r}` pattern.
4. Keep `main()` so `python test_*.py -p <platform>` still works, as the
   converted `prefetch_async_demo` does.

`sdma_async_completion_demo` is the natural first one: it already carries
`@pytest.mark.sdma` from #1609, so its capability and ordering are expressible
today and only the body needs moving.

Doing it one file at a time is safe — the two forms coexist in the tree already.

### Priority

Low (no impact today, good to fix eventually)

---

Related: #1604 (scene-test CI cost — different root cause, same subsystem).
Found while scoping the follow-up named in #1609's commit message; that message
called the conversion "a larger change", which is accurate about size but
implied a framework limitation that does not exist.

## #1639 [Code Health] Deduplicate jobs between ci.yml and ci-self-cpu.yml workflows

- State: closed
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1639
- Created: 2026-08-02T10:24:47Z
- Updated: 2026-08-04T02:56:01Z
- Closed: 2026-08-04T02:56:01Z

### Body

### Category

Technical Debt (cleanup, refactor)

### Component

Other (please specify in description) — `.github/workflows/` CI workflows

### Description

`ci-self-cpu.yml` (the emergency CPU lane) duplicates large parts of `ci.yml`:

1. **`detect-changes` job** — the NON_CODE vocabulary + all gating axes are copied verbatim between the two workflows. This has already drifted **twice**: `examples_only` never reached the lane (#1607) and `tests_only` did not either (#1635). `.claude/rules/ci-change-detection.md` now mandates "any change to an axis means two files, same commit" plus a two-file outputs-consistency grep — a permanent sync tax on every gate change.
2. **T1 no-hardware jobs** (pre-commit, ut, packaging, profiling-flags-smoke, st-sim-a2a3/a5) and **T3 NPU jobs** (ut-a2a3, st-onboard-a2a3, ut-a5, st-onboard-a5) exist in both workflows, differing only in runner selection and setup (ci.yml: `setup-python` + no venv; lane: plain venv + pip cache; both wrap NPU tests in `task-submit`).
3. **Per-job scaffolding** — checkout-with-`repository`/`ref`, `Cache pip packages`, and venv creation steps are repeated across the lane's 10+ jobs.

Every change to a gate axis or a job's steps must be made twice; the drift history is already two incidents. The lane's own header comment and the rules file both carry "keep the two in sync" notes.

### Location

- `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
- `.github/workflows/ci-self-cpu.yml`
- `.claude/rules/ci-change-detection.md` (documents the sync requirement)

### Proposed Fix

- **Highest value: extract `detect-changes` into one canonical implementation** (a reusable workflow via `workflow_call` or a composite action) consumed by both `ci.yml` and `ci-self-cpu.yml`, eliminating the two-copy drift. The rule's outputs-consistency grep then checks one file.
- **Parameterize the job bodies**: a reusable workflow whose caller passes the differences as inputs — `runs-on` targets, setup variant (setup-python path vs plain-venv + pip cache), arch selection. T1/T3 job definitions exist once.
- **Extract the repeated step blocks** (checkout-with-ref, pip cache, venv) into composite actions.
- Constraint: the lane must stay triggerable via `workflow_call` from the `/run-cpu` button under the fork-PR read-only token, and via `workflow_dispatch` for manual runs — reusable workflows are compatible with both.

### Priority

Medium (no impact today, but the duplication has already caused two gating drifts)

## #1642 [Code Health] Device-phase/strace timing buffer is copied device↔host on every simpler_run, unconditionally and unaffected by its own enable gates

- State: closed
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1642
- Created: 2026-08-03T03:38:44Z
- Updated: 2026-08-05T09:23:33Z
- Closed: 2026-08-05T09:23:33Z

### Body

### Category

Technical Debt (cleanup, refactor)

### Component

Host Runtime

### Description

Every `simpler_run` (i.e. every round / every token on the decode hot path) performs **three device↔host transfers** around the AICPU device-phase / strace timing buffer, and **all three run unconditionally**, even though the only consumer of that data is gated off by two separate switches.

Per-run transfers:

| # | Operation | Direction | Payload |
| - | --------- | --------- | ------- |
| 1 | `ensure_device_wall_buffer()` H2D reset | Host→Device | whole buffer reset to sentinel |
| 2 | `read_device_wall_ns()` first `rtMemcpy` | Device→Host | AICPU phase region (`kThreads × NUM_AICPU_PHASES`) |
| 3 | `read_device_wall_ns()` second `rtMemcpy` | Device→Host | task-timing tail (`kThreads × NUM_TASK_TIMING_SLOTS`) |

Payload sizes (16 B/record):

- **a2a3** (`kThreads = 6`): phase region 960 B, tail 1536 B; H2D reset 2496 B.
- **a5** (`kThreads = 14`): phase region 2240 B, tail 3584 B; H2D reset 5824 B.

Two observations about how this data is used vs. how it is transferred:

1. **The transfers are not gated, but the consumer is.** The only reader of `last_device_wall_ns()` / `last_device_phase_ns()` / `last_task_slot_*()` is `emit_device_phase_markers()`, which is double-gated: compile-time `SIMPLER_HOST_STRACE` (so `STRACE_DEV_SPAN_AT` compiles to nothing when off) and runtime `device_profiling_enabled()` (env `SIMPLER_DEVICE_STRACE_ENABLE != 0`). Neither `read_device_wall_ns()` nor `ensure_device_wall_buffer()` checks either gate — the only guard is `if (device_wall_dev_ptr_ == nullptr) return`, and the buffer is lazily allocated once and stays non-null. So with `SIMPLER_DEVICE_STRACE_ENABLE=0` all three transfers still happen every run and the data read back is discarded.

2. **The task-timing tail is opt-in per task but copied every run.** The tail (transfer #3, larger than the phase region on both arches) only holds data for tasks explicitly tagged via `set_task_timing_slot` (default `TASK_TIMING_SLOT_NONE`). Runs that tag no task — the common case — still pay the full tail D2H, reading back all-sentinel records.

Confirmed there is no other consumer of this data (no Python binding / benchmark return value reads it; grep of `python/bindings` is empty), so the readback exists purely to feed the strace markers.

This is per-run end-to-end latency on the dispatch/decode path, so it matters most on short-run, high-frequency workloads.

Verified on `upstream/main` at `a93a331fbfa2adfa02ea0e289cd61c08e20be2d5`.

### Location

- `src/common/platform/onboard/host/device_runner_base.cpp:1213` — `ensure_device_wall_buffer()` (per-run H2D reset)
- `src/common/platform/onboard/host/device_runner_base.cpp:1348` — `read_device_wall_ns()` (two D2H `rtMemcpy`, lines `1369` and `1407`)
- `src/a2a3/platform/onboard/host/device_runner.cpp:269` / `:619` — per-run call sites (a2a3)
- `src/a5/platform/onboard/host/device_runner.cpp:185` / `:442` — per-run call sites (a5)
- `src/common/platform/onboard/host/c_api_shared.cpp:470` — `device_profiling_enabled()` (env gate on the consumer)
- `src/common/platform/onboard/host/c_api_shared.cpp:484` — `emit_device_phase_markers()` (sole consumer of the readback)

### Priority

Low (no impact today, good to fix eventually)

## #1645 [Feature] Raise CHIP_MAX_TENSOR_ARGS above 128 for composed L2 callables

- State: closed
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1645
- Created: 2026-08-03T06:51:50Z
- Updated: 2026-08-03T12:52:47Z
- Closed: 2026-08-03T12:52:47Z

### Body

## Summary

Raise the chip-level tensor argument capacity from 128 to at least 192, or
replace the fixed cap with scalable/configurable storage, so that realistic
composed L2 callables can be dispatched without artificial splitting.

This is a follow-up to #786 / #788, which raised the previous limit from 64 to
128.

## Motivation

While composing the DeepSeek V4 MTP decode path into a single L2 callable, the
combined entry needs 164 tensor parameters:

1. main-model decode;
2. device-side MTP verification and token packing;
3. MTP draft decode.

The generated callable fails during startup with:

```text
ValueError: make_callable: sig_count exceeds MaxSig
```

The current limit is:

```cpp
inline constexpr int CHIP_MAX_TENSOR_ARGS = 128;
```

Because 164 exceeds this limit, the downstream implementation had to retain two
L2 submissions:

- L2 1: main decode + MTP verification/packing;
- L2 2: MTP draft decode.

Downstream references:

- https://github.com/hw-native-sys/pypto-lib/pull/884
- https://github.com/hw-native-sys/pypto-serving/pull/133

The validated 3-to-2 L2 reduction lowered steady critical-rank host decode time
from 45.159 ms to 42.980 ms. Supporting a single L2 would allow us to evaluate
removing the remaining dispatch, bind, runner and output-validation boundary.
No additional latency improvement is claimed until a comparable 2-to-1
benchmark is available.

## Requested change

Please consider one of the following:

1. raise `CHIP_MAX_TENSOR_ARGS` to at least 192, leaving some headroom above the
   current 164-argument reproducer; or
2. make chip-level argument storage scalable or configurable so smaller models
   do not pay the maximum fixed-storage cost.

The change should cover all storage and transport points derived from the cap,
including:

- `ChipCallable::signature_`;
- `ChipStorageTaskArgs`;
- runtime `L2TaskArgs`;
- Python `make_callable` bindings;
- hierarchical-worker mailbox sizing and its capacity `static_assert`;
- relevant a2a3/a5 and sim/onboard paths.

Please also add a regression test that accepts a 164-tensor callable and rejects
`CHIP_MAX_TENSOR_ARGS + 1` with an error containing both the requested and
supported tensor counts.

## Capacity considerations

`Tensor` is currently 128 bytes, so raising the fixed capacity from 128 to 192
adds approximately 8 KiB to each fixed tensor-argument storage object.

The hierarchical-worker mailbox is currently 32 KiB and is statically sized to
hold the maximum accepted `TaskArgs` blob. A 192-tensor capacity may still fit,
but the complete layout including `CallConfig`, scalar arguments, headers,
alignment and the error region should be verified. A 256-tensor choice would
likely require a larger mailbox or out-of-line argument storage.

## Expected behavior

A composed callable with 164 tensor parameters should compile, upload and
dispatch successfully on supported a2a3/a5 sim and onboard runtimes, without
requiring a model-specific argument-packing workaround or an extra L2 boundary.

## #1646 [Docs] host_build_graph docs and comments describe a runtime model the code no longer implements

- State: closed
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1646
- Created: 2026-08-03T07:17:50Z
- Updated: 2026-08-04T08:00:08Z
- Closed: 2026-08-04T08:00:08Z

### Body

### Documentation Location

`host_build_graph` (a2a3). Verified against `upstream/main` @ `810fbcd117ac92a1ff0412b3c29fda12c2c1d01e`.

- `src/a2a3/runtime/host_build_graph/docs/SCALAR_DATA_ACCESS.md` — §1, §3.2 (L44), §4 table (L109), §5 (L123)
- `src/a2a3/runtime/host_build_graph/docs/RUNTIME_LOGIC.md` — L300 (Sizing guideline), L362
- `src/a2a3/runtime/host_build_graph/orchestration/pto_orchestration_api.h` — L313
- `src/a2a3/runtime/host_build_graph/runtime/pto_runtime2_types.h` — L148
- `src/a2a3/runtime/host_build_graph/runtime/orchestrator_core/pto_runtime2.cpp` — L110
- `src/a2a3/runtime/host_build_graph/runtime/orchestrator_core/pto_orchestrator.cpp` — L423

### What's Wrong or Missing?

`host_build_graph`'s documentation and several load-bearing code comments still describe a runtime model the code no longer implements. Three separate facets, all pre-existing on `main`.

---

#### 1. Removed dependency mechanism (`fanout_refcount`) is still presented as current behavior

The wiring/refcount dependency model was replaced by the polling model (`completion_flags` + `completed_watermark`). The refcount fields are gone — `fanout_refcount`, `fanin_refcount`, `fanout_head`, `fanout_count`, and `PTO2_FANOUT_SCOPE_BIT` have **zero field declarations** anywhere under `src/a2a3/runtime/host_build_graph/`, yet **34 references** to them remain.

Most are correct historical notes ("on_task_release is gone under polling… that signal is now the per-ring `completed_watermark`", `pto_scheduler.h:878`) and read fine. The following seven, however, state a removed mechanism as present-tense fact:

| Location | Text | Actual mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SCALAR_DATA_ACCESS.md:44` | "wait for all consumers to finish (`fanout_refcount >= fanout_count - 1`, excluding the scope reference)" | `completed_watermark > last_consumer_local_id` |
| `SCALAR_DATA_ACCESS.md:109` | table row: "spin-wait fanout_refcount" | same as above |
| `SCALAR_DATA_ACCESS.md:123` | "INOUT registers a producer entry in TensorMap, enabling `set_tensor_data` to track all consumers through `fanout_refcount`" | same as above |
| `pto_orchestration_api.h:313` | "INOUT creates a TensorMap entry that enables automatic consumer tracking via `fanout_refcount`" | same as above |
| `pto_runtime2_types.h:148` | state machine: `COMPLETED->CONSUMED: fanout_refcount == fanout_count && state == COMPLETED` | no refcount participates |
| `pto_runtime2.cpp:110` | file-header comment: "(consumer low bits of `fanout_refcount` >= consumer count, excluding the …)" | same as above |
| `pto_orchestrator.cpp:423` | lists zeroed fields including `fanout_refcount=0` | field does not exist |

`pto_orchestration_api.h` is the header orchestration authors read directly, so a reader can reasonably act on L313.

---

#### 2. `SCALAR_DATA_ACCESS.md` §1 states a capability `host_build_graph` does not have

> During task graph construction, orchestration sometimes needs to **read InCore kernel results (for control-flow decisions)** or write initial values into tensors.

That is true for `tensormap_and_ringbuffer`, whose orchestrator runs on the AICPU concurrently with the schedulers. It is **not** true for `host_build_graph`: `run_host_orchestration()` runs the whole orchestration on the host, then `copy_to_device()` uploads the populated SM, and only then does the AICPU kernel boot scheduler-only (`aicpu_executor.cpp` — "host_build_graph has no device-side orchestrator"). No device task has executed during orchestration, so a producer's `task_state` can never reach `COMPLETED` and `wait_for_tensor_ready` spins to `PTO2_TENSOR_DATA_TIMEOUT_CYCLES` (15 s) before failing with `PTO2_ERROR_TENSOR_WAIT_TIMEOUT`.

The restriction is currently recorded only in a scene-test comment — `tests/st/a2a3/host_build_graph/available_aicore_counts/kernels/orchestration/available_aicore_counts_orch.cpp:75-79`:

```cpp
// shape carries no producer or consumer task, so set_tensor_data writes it
// straight through. Giving it one would hang host_build_graph: its
// orchestrator runs to completion on the host before the device executes
// anything, so a producer's task_state can never reach COMPLETED and
// wait_for_tensor_ready would spin to PTO2_TENSOR_DATA_TIMEOUT_CYCLES.
```

Both `host_build_graph` users of these APIs (`available_aicore_counts`, `paged_attention`) only touch tensors with no producer, which is the path that works. A reader who follows §1 instead gets a failure that surfaces 15 s later under an error code that does not point at the root cause. The doc lives under `host_build_graph/docs/` and carries no note of this difference.

---

#### 3. `RUNTIME_LOGIC.md` sizing guideline is scoped per-`PTO2_SCOPE`, and quotes a default that does not match the code

L300:

> **Sizing guideline**: `task_window_size` must be larger than the maximum number of tasks in any single `PTO2_SCOPE`. A safe choice is `2 × max_tasks_per_scope` or simply the default 65536 for production.

Two problems:

- **Scope of the constraint.** `host_build_graph` is whole-graph-resident and never advances `last_task_alive` (`pto_scheduler.h:26` — "reclaim (whole-graph-resident), so `last_task_alive` is not advanced here"). The ring allocator's gate is `local_task_id_ - last_alive + 1 < window_size_` (`pto_ring_buffer.h:145`); with `last_alive` pinned at 0 that becomes `local_task_id_ + 1 < window_size_`, so the effective cap is the **total task count of the whole graph**, not the largest scope. Sizing by `2 × max_tasks_per_scope` on a graph with many small scopes under-sizes the window, and the allocator then spins waiting for a reclaim that never happens.
- **Default value.** The doc says `65536` here and again at L362 (`task_window=65536`); the code is `#define PTO2_TASK_WINDOW_SIZE 16384` (`pto_runtime2_types.h:73`).

### Additional Context

- Found incidentally while reviewing #1618. **Everything above is pre-existing on `main` and independent of that PR** — no finding here is introduced by it.
- Only `src/a2a3/runtime/host_build_graph/` was swept. `tensormap_and_ringbuffer`, the top-level `docs/`, and `a5` were not checked and may carry similar residue from the same migration.
- Reproduce the residue counts with:

  ```bash
  for sym in fanout_refcount fanin_refcount fanout_head fanout_count PTO2_FANOUT_SCOPE_BIT; do
    printf '%-24s decls:%s refs:%s\n' "$sym" \
      "$(git grep -cE "(int32_t|uint32_t|uint64_t|std::atomic<[^>]*>)\s+$sym" -- src/a2a3/runtime/host_build_graph/ | wc -l)" \
      "$(git grep -c "$sym" -- src/a2a3/runtime/host_build_graph/ | awk -F: '{s+=$NF} END{print s+0}')"
  done
  ```

- Per `.claude/rules/doc-consistency.md`, doc updates are the responsibility of the commit that changes the code; that rule does not cover drift that already exists, which is why this is filed separately.

## #1656 [Code Health] Task-timing tail is copied D2H every profiling run even when no task is tagged

- State: closed
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1656
- Created: 2026-08-03T09:33:25Z
- Updated: 2026-08-06T12:19:51Z
- Closed: 2026-08-06T12:19:51Z

### Body

Follow-up to #1642 (observation 2), split out because it is a materially larger, device-touching change than the host-only gate that #1642 landed.

### Context

#1642 gated the three per-run device↔host transfers around the AICPU device-phase / task-timing buffer on `device_phase_capture_enabled()` (compile `SIMPLER_HOST_STRACE` + runtime `SIMPLER_DEVICE_STRACE_ENABLE`). That eliminates all three transfers in the production common case (capture off).

This issue is the residual: **when capture is ON but this run tags no task**, the task-timing *tail* D2H (`read_device_wall_ns()`'s second `rtMemcpy`, the larger of the two readbacks — a2a3 1536 B, a5 3584 B) still runs and reads back all-sentinel records.

The tail is opt-in per task: only tasks tagged via `set_task_timing_slot` (default `TASK_TIMING_SLOT_NONE`) are folded into it by the scheduler; untagged tasks never touch it. But the host reads the whole tail unconditionally whenever capture is on.

### Proposed design

Add a host-readable **"any task tagged"** marker so the host reads the marker first and copies the tail only when it is set:

1. **Marker (uniform, `device_phase.h`):** a `tail_used` word in a small header at the front of the device buffer; shift the phase-region / tail offsets via the existing `*_offset()` / `*_bytes()` helpers (keep 16-byte record alignment). Host reads it as part of the phase-region D2H it *already* does (transfer #2), then gates the tail D2H (transfer #3) on it. Host reset zeroes it.

2. **Device write (non-uniform — the real cost):** written once, off the dispatch hot path, deduped, at a run-epilogue point ("orch submitted all tasks" / "scheduler done"). The write point differs per runtime tree:
   - `tensormap_and_ringbuffer` (a2a3, a5): has a clean `SchedWindow` / `OrchWindow` close hook (`scheduler_cold_path.cpp` / `aicpu_executor.cpp`).
   - `host_build_graph` (a2a3): tagged branch in `scheduler/scheduler_context.h`, **no** device sched/orch phase (orch runs on host) — different teardown.
   - `host_build_graph` (a5): tail path lives in `aicpu/aicpu_executor.cpp` — yet another structure.

   So the marker write needs a per-tree landing across all four runtime trees, plus sim parity, and lands as one commit with the wire-layout change (all readers/writers move together).

### Why it is a follow-up, not part of #1642

The payoff lands **only while profiling is actively on** (capture-off is fully handled by #1642). Weighed against a wire-layout change + device-side edits across four near-duplicate-but-not-identical runtime trees, it is a separate, self-contained piece of work.

### Priority

Low (no production impact; only trims a readback during active profiling sessions).

---

## #1690 [Bug] L3 multi-rank STRACE records interleave on shared stderr and corrupt benchmark timing

- State: closed
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1690
- Created: 2026-08-04T12:38:03Z
- Updated: 2026-08-06T01:00:43Z
- Closed: 2026-08-06T01:00:43Z

### Body

### Platform

a2a3 (Ascend 910B/C hardware)

### Runtime Variant

tensormap_and_ringbuffer

### Description

L3 multi-rank benchmark timing is unreliable because forked chip-worker processes write `[STRACE]` records concurrently to the same captured `stderr` file descriptor.

`HostLogger::emit` writes one logical log record through multiple stdio calls. Its mutex is local to each `HostLogger` instance and therefore does not serialize writers from different forked processes. Records from different ranks can consequently be interleaved into the same physical line.

The STRACE parser extracts only one record from each physical line. Interleaved records are therefore lost, causing:

- Missing orchestrator or scheduler spans
- `effective_us=0.0` for valid dispatches
- Fewer reported ranks than the actual world size
- Unstable and systematically inflated median/mean latency

The MoE computation itself completes successfully and passes correctness checks. This is an instrumentation output problem, not a kernel performance regression.

### Steps to Reproduce

Use the following configuration:

```bash
source <CANN_INSTALLATION>/set_env.sh

export PYTHONPATH=<WORKSPACE>/pypto-lib
export TORCH_DEVICE_BACKEND_AUTOLOAD=0
export PYPTO_BENCH=1
export PYPTO_BENCH_WARMUP=2
export PYPTO_BENCH_ROUNDS=8
export PYPTO_BENCH_RAW=1
export DSV4_HC_PRE_IMPL=separate
export PYPTO_ROUTE_HASH_IMPL=aiv
export PTO2_RING_DEP_POOL=16384
export PTO2_RING_TASK_WINDOW=16384
export PTO2_RING_HEAP=1073741824

.venv/bin/python models/deepseek/v4-flash/moe.py \
    -p a2a3 \
    --ep 8 \
    -d 0,2,4,6,8,10,12,14 \
    --balanced-routing \
    --enable-l2-swimlane 0
```

Parallel configuration:

- Expert parallel size: 8
- World size: 8
- Participating devices: `0,2,4,6,8,10,12,14`
- Mapping: rank 0 -> device 0, rank 1 -> device 2, ..., rank 7 -> device 14
- Warmup rounds: 2
- Measured rounds: 8
- Routing: balanced
- HcPre implementation: separate
- Route hash implementation: AIV

The issue reproduces consistently in three independent runs.

### Expected Behavior

For 8 ranks and 8 measured rounds:

- All 64 `(rank, round)` cells should contain a valid `effective_us` value.
- The reported rank count should be 8.
- Median and mean latency should remain stable across repeated runs.
- Results should be comparable with the approximately 477 us reference baseline for this configuration.
- Missing STRACE spans should be reported as invalid instrumentation data rather than silently converted to `0.0`.

### Actual Behavior

All three runs complete successfully in approximately 35-44 seconds. Correctness passes with `x_next ratio_reldiff < 0.003`.

There are no runtime errors, timeouts, or device failures: no `507018`, `507014`, `507899`, `HandleTaskTimeout`, or `FATAL` records.

However, most benchmark timing samples are missing:

| Run | Reported ranks | Non-zero samples out of 64 | Minimum effective_us | Median effective_us | host_union_mean |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| v3 | 7 | 14 | 476.0 us | unavailable | 2773 us |
| v4 | 7 | 13 | 476.1 us | 958.8 us | 2678 us |
| v5 | 8 | 20 | 472.8 us | 1210.6 us | 2631 us |

In v5, all eight participating ranks contain missing `0.0` cells. One participating worker has all eight measured rounds reported as `0.0`.

The minimum non-zero values from the three runs agree with the approximately 477 us reference within about 1%, indicating that kernel performance itself is not regressed. The median and mean values are corrupted by missing or incorrectly parsed spans.

### Git Commit ID

`simpler`: `9922afdb08cc6f203eaf39328661e2f2648d333d`

Related versions:

- `pypto-lib`: `fc9993fb26732bc1e718d952f65abc6b3fa2a227`
- `pypto`: `1784c635b5ea750c5666dde0fe132aa2c1d10a34`
- `pto-isa`: `83d01313d9bfc247c4b7c8bcf969d1019f0d106f`
- PTOAS: `0.48`
- `pypto-serving`: not used

### CANN Version

9.0.0, timestamp 20260428

### Driver Version

26.0.rc1

Firmware version is not reported by the board. The reported software version is 26.0.rc1.

### Host Platform

Linux (aarch64)

- OS: openEuler 24.03 SP1
- Kernel: `6.6.0-72.0.0.76.oe2403sp1.aarch64`
- Python: 3.11.6
- PyTorch: 2.8.0+cpu
- NumPy: 2.2.6
- NPU: Ascend910, Product `IT22HMDA_2_S`
- PCI Device ID: `0xD803`
- HBM: 64 GB per chip

### Additional Context

#### Root-cause evidence

At the affected commit, `src/common/log/host_log.cpp:86-92` emits one logical record using several operations:

```cpp
fprintf(stderr, ...);
vfprintf(stderr, fmt, args);
fputc('\n', stderr);
fflush(stderr);
```

The surrounding `std::scoped_lock` protects only threads using the same `HostLogger` instance. Each forked L3 chip-worker process has its own logger and mutex, so it does not prevent cross-process writes to the shared captured `stderr` descriptor.

In `simpler_setup/tools/strace_timing.py:51-55,98-113`, `parse_spans` performs one `_STRACE_RE.search` per physical line. The greedy `attrs=.*` portion can consume the remainder of a line containing another interleaved STRACE record. The second record is not recovered.

When an orchestrator or scheduler span is lost, the benchmark reports `effective_us=0.0`. If all samples for a rank are lost, that rank is omitted from the reported rank count.

#### Suggested fixes

1. Format each host log record into a contiguous buffer and emit it with one cross-process-safe write. STRACE records written to a captured pipe should remain within `PIPE_BUF` so each record is atomic.
2. Harden `parse_spans` to detect multiple STRACE markers or malformed interleaved records instead of silently accepting partial input.
3. Validate the expected rank and round counts before calculating statistics.
4. Mark missing spans as invalid samples and report an instrumentation error; do not represent them as `0.0`.
5. Add an L3 multi-process test in which several child processes concurrently emit STRACE records to the same captured descriptor.

#### Workaround

Capture each rank's `stderr` into a separate file and parse the files independently before aggregating benchmark results. `PYPTO_BENCH_RAW=1` alone does not prevent shared-descriptor interleaving.

## #1697 [Bug] sim device log splits one record across three stdio calls, so concurrent AICPU threads and forked chip workers interleave partial records

- State: closed
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1697
- Created: 2026-08-05T07:38:17Z
- Updated: 2026-08-06T06:32:30Z
- Closed: 2026-08-06T06:32:30Z

### Body

### Platform

All / Unknown — precisely: **a2a3sim + a5sim**. The defect is in the shared file `src/common/platform/sim/aicpu/device_log.cpp`, so both sim variants are affected identically. **Onboard (`a2a3` / `a5`) is not affected** — see Additional Context.

### Runtime Variant

All / Unknown — the sim device-log backend sits at the platform layer and is used by both `tensormap_and_ringbuffer` and `host_build_graph`.

### Description

The sim platform's device-log backend emits **one logical log record via three separate stdio calls**, with **no lock at all**:

```cpp
// src/common/platform/sim/aicpu/device_log.cpp:61-65 (dev_vlog_debug; info/timing/warn/error identical)
void dev_vlog_debug(const char *func, const char *fmt, va_list args) {
    fprintf(stderr, "[DEBUG] %s: ", func);
    vfprintf(stderr, fmt, args);
    fputc('\n', stderr);
}
```

glibc locks the `FILE` for each individual call, but **not across the three-call sequence**. Any concurrent writer can therefore land its own output between the level/func prefix, the message body, and the terminating newline — producing records that are merged onto one physical line or split across two.

There are two independent concurrency sources in sim, and **only one of them requires `fork`**:

1. **Intra-process, multi-threaded (the easy one).** Sim runs AICPU as host threads — `SimDeviceRunnerBase::create_thread` (`src/common/platform/sim/host/device_runner_base.cpp:240`) spawns up to `aicpu_thread_num` workers (`PLATFORM_MAX_AICPU_THREADS` = 4 on a2a3, 7 on a5). Every one of those threads calls `dev_vlog_*` on the same `stderr`. **No `fork` needed — a single sim process with `aicpu_thread_num > 1` is enough.**
2. **Cross-process, forked chip workers.** `python/simpler/worker.py` forks chip children (`_chip_process_loop`, `_forked_child_main`) for sim exactly as it does for onboard; the children share the parent's captured `stderr` file descriptor.

This is the **same defect class as #1690** (host-side `HostLogger::emit` writing one record via `fprintf` + `vfprintf` + `fputc` + `fflush`). PR #1691 fixed it for the **host** backend only — it buffers each record into a contiguous `std::string` and emits it with a single `::write(STDERR_FILENO, ...)`. The sim device backend was left unchanged, so the defect survives in `src/common/platform/sim/`.

Notably, sim is **strictly worse than the pre-#1691 host path**: `HostLogger` at least held a process-local `std::mutex` around its stdio sequence, so single-process multi-threaded output stayed intact. The sim `dev_vlog_*` functions hold nothing, so they interleave even without `fork`.

### Steps to Reproduce

**Multi-threaded path (no fork required):**

1. Pick a sim scene test configured with more than one AICPU thread, e.g. `tests/st/a5/tensormap_and_ringbuffer/mixed_example/` (`"config": {"aicpu_thread_num": 4}`) or `tests/st/a5/tensormap_and_ringbuffer/mx_fp_gemm/` (`aicpu_thread_num: 2`).
2. Run it in sim with the device log opened up so several AICPU threads log concurrently, capturing `stderr`:

   ```bash
   pytest tests/st/a5/tensormap_and_ringbuffer/mixed_example \
       --platform a5sim --log-level debug 2>capture.log
   ```

3. Inspect `capture.log` for torn records — lines carrying two level tags, or a `[TIMING]`/`[DEBUG]` prefix with no message body following it:

   ```bash
   grep -cE '\[(DEBUG|INFO|TIMING|WARN|ERROR)\].*\[(DEBUG|INFO|TIMING|WARN|ERROR)\]' capture.log
   grep -nE '\[(DEBUG|INFO|TIMING|WARN|ERROR)\] [A-Za-z_~][A-Za-z0-9_:~]*: *$' capture.log
   ```

Being a race, the hit rate scales with log volume and thread count; `--log-level debug` with `aicpu_thread_num` at the platform maximum is the strongest signal.

**Deterministic regression test.** PR #1691 added exactly the right harness shape for the host side in `tests/ut/cpp/a5/test_host_log_off.cpp::ForkedProcessesEmitWholePipeRecords` (16 forked children x 128 records through a shared pipe, verifying one record per physical line). The same test, retargeted at `dev_vlog_*` and extended with a pure multi-threaded variant, is the natural regression barrier here.

### Expected Behavior

Each `dev_vlog_*` call produces exactly one intact physical line on `stderr`, regardless of how many AICPU sim threads or forked chip-worker processes are writing concurrently. This is what both sibling backends already guarantee:

- **onboard** (`src/common/platform/onboard/aicpu/device_log.cpp:53-55`) buffers into a single `char buffer[2048]` and issues one `dlog_*` call;
- **host, after #1691** (`src/common/log/host_log.cpp`) buffers into one `std::string` and issues one `::write`.

### Actual Behavior

Records from concurrent AICPU sim threads and forked chip workers interleave on the shared `stderr`, producing merged or split lines. Consequences:

- Device log records become unparseable or silently lost by any line-oriented consumer.
- The `SIMPLER_DFX` `Total` / `Orch` / `Sched` markers and `log_stall_diagnostics` output can be corrupted, which is the failure mode that makes device-log triage untrustworthy in the first place (`.claude/rules/running-onboard.md` documents these as the ground truth for stall/deadlock classification).
- Sim runs of a benchmark are exposed to the same class of instrumentation corruption #1690 reported for onboard host output — with the added wrinkle that in sim it needs no multi-rank setup, just `aicpu_thread_num > 1`.

The kernels themselves compute correctly; this is purely an instrumentation-output defect.

### Git Commit ID

c866c827e40b798a4629cf1139d41d430d9eb88e (`upstream/main`; `src/common/platform/sim/aicpu/device_log.cpp` is untouched by PR #1691)

### Host Platform

Linux (aarch64)

### Additional Context

**Backend comparison — sim is the only one that splits a record:**

| Backend | Emit mechanism | One record per call? |
| :------ | :------------- | :------------------- |
| onboard device (`onboard/aicpu/device_log.cpp`) | `vsnprintf` into `char buffer[2048]`, then one `dlog_*` | Yes |
| host (`src/common/log/host_log.cpp`), after #1691 | format into `std::string`, then one `::write` | Yes |
| **sim device (`sim/aicpu/device_log.cpp`)** | **`fprintf` + `vfprintf` + `fputc`, unlocked** | **No** |

**Suggested fix.** Apply the shape the other two backends already use — format into a contiguous buffer, emit once. Keeping the record within `PIPE_BUF` preserves cross-process atomicity when `stderr` is a shared captured pipe, the same property PR #1691 relies on. `docs/logging.md:142` currently describes the sim backend as "buffer-free (single `vfprintf(stderr, ...)`)"; that line is inaccurate today (there are three calls, not one) and would need updating alongside the fix per `.claude/rules/doc-consistency.md`.

Note that `dev_vlog_*` is on the AICPU logging path, so the fix must not introduce per-call heap allocation — a stack buffer sized like onboard's `char buffer[2048]` plus a single `fwrite`/`write` keeps the cost at or below today's, and `.claude/rules/codestyle.md` §7 already forbids logging on AICPU hot paths, so the volume is bounded by design.

Related: #1690 (host-side variant of this defect), #1691 (fix for the host side only).

Found while reviewing PR #1691.

## #1698 [Code Health] Remove unreachable args-dump arena overwrite-detection after backpressure lands (#1662)

- State: open
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1698
- Created: 2026-08-05T08:49:43Z
- Updated: 2026-08-05T08:49:43Z
- Closed: 

### Body

> Depends on #1662. This becomes actionable only **after** the arena-backpressure protocol in #1662 lands, because that PR is what makes the host-side overwrite path unreachable.

### Category
Dead Code / Unused Dependencies

### Component
Host Runtime

### Description
Before #1662, the args-dump host collector detected arena wrap-around
overwrites: when a per-thread circular arena wrapped and the device
overwrote payload bytes the host had not yet drained, the collector
flagged the record with `overwritten = true`, bumped
`total_overwrite_count_`, and skipped writing its (corrupted) payload to
`args.bin`.

#1662 makes the device block *before* any reuse write: on every arena
wrap (write-full or cross-arena-end) `ensure_dump_arena_capacity()` marks
`fq_contended`, waits for the host freeze/release, and spins until
`completed_payload_count >= target` before advancing `arena_write_offset`.
The timeout path drops the record and returns `-1` **without** advancing
the offset. So under the new protocol the device never overwrites
un-drained payload, and the host-side overwrite branch is unreachable —
dead code.

Keeping the dead branch also leaves a **latent count-divergence trap**:
the device counts a payload as published when `kind==TENSOR &&
payload_size>0`, while the host only counts it written when additionally
`!overwritten`. If the `overwritten` branch ever fired, `written[t]`
would fall permanently behind `published[t]`, `backpressure_release_ready()`
would never return true, and the freeze would stall until the AICPU
timeout. Removing the now-unreachable branch also removes this divergence
hazard.

**Trade-off to weigh before deleting:** the `overwritten` detection today
doubles as a *corruption smoke-detector* — if the backpressure protocol
ever regressed, this branch is what would surface "host drain slower than
arena reuse" instead of silently emitting bad bytes. Options:
1. Delete the branch, `overwritten` field, and `total_overwrite_count_`
   entirely (treat #1662 as the invariant).
2. Keep a cheap assertion/`LOG_ERROR` that fires if the (should-be-dead)
   condition is ever observed, but drop the field/manifest plumbing.

Recommend deciding between (1) and (2) as part of this cleanup.

### Location
- `src/common/platform/shared/host/args_dump_collector.cpp` — `process_dump_buffer()` overwrite-detection block (`dt.overwritten = ...`, `total_overwrite_count_` bump, `has_payload` gating on `!dt.overwritten`)
- `src/common/platform/include/host/args_dump_collector.h` — `total_overwrite_count_` member and any manifest/export surface
- `src/common/platform/include/common/args_dump.h` — `overwritten` record/DumpedArg field (if unused elsewhere after removal)
- `docs/dfx/args-dump.md` — §7.2 already rewritten by #1662; scrub any residual `overwritten` references

### Proposed Fix
After #1662 merges, remove the unreachable host-side overwrite-detection
path (or downgrade it to a bare assertion per option 2 above), drop the
associated `total_overwrite_count_` accounting and the `overwritten`
field where it becomes unused, and update `docs/dfx/args-dump.md`
accordingly. Verify the a2a3/a5 args-dump UTs and sim scene tests still
pass.

### Priority
Low (no impact today, good to fix eventually)

## #1706 [Tracking] host_build_graph — intent, vision & change tracking

- State: open
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1706
- Created: 2026-08-06T03:28:12Z
- Updated: 2026-08-06T07:17:06Z
- Closed: 

### Body

This issue tracks **all `host_build_graph` (HBG) work, on a2a3 and a5** — what the runtime
is for, where it stands today, and the open work. Individual items are attached as
**sub-issues** below (the panel auto-updates as items are added or closed).

**Scope: a2a3 and a5.** HBG is one runtime with two arch trees, kept in sync. A sub-issue is
about HBG, not about an arch — file one, not two. See
[Per-arch divergence](#divergence) for when that stops being true.

## What HBG is

HBG separates graph construction from device execution
(`src/{arch}/runtime/host_build_graph/docs/RUNTIME_LOGIC.md` §1):

```text
host: dlopen the orchestration SO, run it to completion → whole task graph
host: relocate the prebuilt graph image, copy it to device memory
device: attach, classify every task once, dispatch with the AICPU schedulers
host: collect outputs, destroy/reset per-run state
```

There is **no device-side orchestrator thread**. The AICPU threads split 3S+1P: the last
thread is a core-less resolution thread (P), the rest own AICore partitions and schedule
them (S). At least two threads are required (#1544). The host constructs the whole graph
before any device task can complete — §1 calls that ordering "the defining constraint of
the runtime", and everything below is a consequence of it.

Structurally HBG is **the host-orchestration variant of `tensormap_and_ringbuffer`**, not a
separate graph model: since #1185 it uses the same `PTO2TaskDescriptor` ring storage and the
same TensorMap-derived dependencies, with one ring and no device orchestrator. (The
"fixed `Task[]` array, up to 131,072 tasks, traverses dependencies" description still in
`src/a2a3/docs/runtimes.md` and in T&R's `RUNTIME_LOGIC.md` §1.1 is stale.)

## Intent and vision

**1. Take orchestration off the AICPU.** No AICPU thread builds the graph, so the whole
device-side thread budget goes to dispatch and completion resolution. Graph construction
runs in ordinary host C++ — full STL, a host debugger, host-side DFX (`dep_gen` is captured
on the host orchestrator, #1492) — and no device-log budget is spent on build-time
diagnostics.

**2. Pair the polling readiness model with the 3S+1P split.** Dependency state is a per-slot
completion flag, a monotonic watermark, intrusive wake lists and inline integer fanin —
no dependency pool, no fanout lock, and no periodic sweep (#1435). That collapses
readiness resolution into one compact sequential job, which is exactly what can be handed
to a single thread: P owns all of it, so it is the sole producer of the ready queues, while
each S thread stays purely core-local — poll its own cores, dispatch them, hand finished
tasks to P over an SPSC queue (#1544). Whole-graph residency is what allows the split: all
threads classify disjoint slices of the finished graph once at boot (#1553), after which no
new task ever arrives. The gain is graph-shaped — a wide parallel graph wins, a serial chain
pays for the extra hop — so quantifying it belongs to the benchmark bucket.

**3. Amortize the host build cost — this is the crux.** Paying for a full host graph build
on every run is only acceptable if repeated work is not rebuilt. Two mechanisms exist:

- **Graph Execution** (`docs/GRAPH_EXECUTION.md`, #1444): a Graph is a composite incore
  task. The first invocation records the DAG; later invocations submit **one** `GRAPH` task
  whose internal nodes the device Scheduler expands from a saved, validated, pointer-free
  POD Definition. Internal nodes consume no ring slots and are never re-submitted by the
  host. This is what makes a repetitive workload (an LLM decoder layer submitted per layer,
  per token) affordable under host orchestration.
- **Prepared-successor pipelining** (#1574, #1540, #1587): preparation of run N+1 overlaps
  with device execution of run N. HBG does *not* overlap orchestration and scheduling
  *within* one run — this is the compensating mechanism.

**4. Where this should land.** `README.md` still positions HBG as the
"development, debugging" runtime against T&R's "production workloads". The vision is that
for **repetitive, statically-shaped** graphs, host orchestration plus Graph replay becomes a
first-class production path rather than the simple-but-slow option — while T&R remains the
runtime for streaming, dynamic, and flow-controlled workloads. Closing that gap is what the
sub-issues here are collectively for, and the README table is one of the last things to
change, not the first.

## Work buckets

Sub-issues attach under these six. The list is the shape of the work, not a schedule.

**1. New features — Graph and Pipeline.**
Graph Execution step 2: every entry in `GRAPH_EXECUTION.md` "Current unsupported cases" is a
candidate sub-issue — dynamic boundary scalars, nested Graphs, dispatch predicates,
runtime-allocated boundary outputs, variable boundary metadata, cross-boundary explicit
dependencies, and the 16-Definition / 1024-node / 32-tensor ceilings. Pipelining: how deep
the slot pipeline should go beyond two, and what remains un-overlapped between runs.

**2. Performance.**
Host build time is now on the critical path. Open work: where a run's wall-clock actually
goes (build vs. relocation vs. H2D vs. device), whether successor pipelining genuinely
hides the build, Graph-replay speedup on a repeated layer, and the whole-graph capacity
model — sizing the task window / heap / fanin / TensorMap pool, and whether anything can
become reusable within a run rather than only at runtime destruction.

**3. Redundant-code removal.**
`SchedulerContext::fanin_satisfied()` has no callers anywhere in the HBG tree. Early
producer propagation and the shared scheduler's early-staging code are retained for T&R
parity but inactive here. Each such path gets a decision — wire it in or delete it — not
indefinite retention.

**4. Naming and documentation conventions.**
The tree is still `pto_*.h` / `PTO2*` throughout; retire it opportunistically per
`.claude/rules/codestyle.md` rules 9–10 — one identifier at a time, inside changes already
touching that code, **no sweep PR**. Documentation and comments that no longer match the
code, in both trees: `RUNTIME_LOGIC.md` §1 and the `aicpu_executor.cpp` dispatch comment
still say every AICPU thread schedules its own cores, which 3S+1P superseded; `dep_pool` /
`DepListPool` comments survive in `runtime/pto_ring_buffer.h`, `pto_shared_memory.h`,
`pto_runtime2.h` and `scheduler/pto_scheduler.h` describing structures #1435 deleted. Also
the stale HBG description in `src/a2a3/docs/runtimes.md`, the broken example path in
`docs/getting-started.md`, and the README positioning once the vision above is realized.

**5. Test-case coverage.**
Scene dirs today: 14 on a2a3 and 4 on a5, against 34 and 33 for T&R. Neither arch has an
`examples/{arch}/host_build_graph/` tree at all. Which T&R scenes have no HBG counterpart,
which a2a3 scenes have no a5 counterpart, and which HBG-specific behaviors (Graph replay,
pipeline slots, capacity exhaustion, the latched error codes) have no scene at all.

**6. Benchmark.**
A repeatable HBG benchmark story: which workloads, which numbers, and against what
baseline — HBG vs. T&R on the same graph, and HBG with vs. without Graph replay. This
depends on DFX parity, so "which of the five DFX features (#995) work on HBG and which are
T&R-only" belongs here, along with the Graph Execution swimlane lanes described in
`GRAPH_EXECUTION.md` §DFX.

## <a name="divergence"></a>Per-arch divergence

Expect deliberate divergence later, where the silicon differs: AICPU thread counts and
topology, AICore geometry, the completion-mailbox ABI, available async engines. One
implementation for both stays the default; a divergence needs a stated hardware reason.

## Open work

See the **sub-issues panel** above — kept current automatically as items are attached or
closed.

## #1708 [Feature] Host swimlane (L3/L4) — the missing third DFX timeline

- State: closed
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1708
- Created: 2026-08-06T03:50:28Z
- Updated: 2026-08-13T01:05:26Z
- Closed: 2026-08-13T01:05:26Z

### Body

### Summary

Add a **host swimlane**: a Perfetto/Chrome-trace timeline of one run's **host-side**
execution (graph build → orchestrator submit → scheduler dispatch → waiting on chip
children → completion), emitted from the `[STRACE]` markers we already produce.

`simpler` has two of the three levels covered (see #995):

| | Level | Answers | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| core swimlane | **L0** | which pipe (`MTE2`/`CUBE`/`FIXP`/…) a task stalls on inside the core | ✅ ships |
| chip swimlane | **L2** | when each task ran on device, and where the AICPU scheduler loop spent its time | ✅ ships |
| **host swimlane** | **L3/L4** | **why a task started when it did** | ❌ **missing** |

The three are successive zoom levels, not alternatives. L2 says "this task ran from t1 to
t2"; L0 says "here is why it was slow inside the core"; **nothing today says why it only
started at t1.**

### Motivation / Use Case

When a run is slower than expected and the device timeline looks fine, there is currently
no timeline to look at. Concretely unanswerable today:

- Did the time go to graph build, to scheduler dispatch, or to waiting on a child?
- Is the host scheduler the bottleneck, and if so is it starved for work or slow to dispatch?
- Did run N+1's host-side preparation actually overlap run N's device execution?
- Why is decode invocation #7 slower than #6?

Two extra reasons this is worth doing as its own feature:

1. **The data already exists.** `[STRACE]` markers already carry real `pid`, real `tid`,
   invocation id, name, `ts`, `dur`, clock, and open-ended `k=v` attributes; host
   timestamps are `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` and **comparable across the parent and its forked
   children**. Unknown `k=v` fields are ignored by the parser, so adding attributes needs
   **no marker-version bump**.
2. **The current viewer discards it.** `strace_timing.py --trace-out` reads the real `tid`
   and then **throws it away**, synthesizing a dense lane id from `(pid, invocation)`.
   Consequences: one lane per *invocation* rather than per *thread*, so a single L4 run
   fans out to `(1 + N_L3 + N_L2) × N_inv` flat lanes, and **spans from one thread get
   split across lanes by invocation** — which is exactly what makes "is #7 slower than #6"
   impossible to see.

### Proposed API / Behavior

New output mode; `--trace-out` stays byte-identical (it is a per-invocation call-tree view,
a legitimate and different question):

```bash
python -m simpler_setup.tools.strace_timing <log> --swimlane host_swimlane.json
# Chrome Trace JSON -> Perfetto, same viewer as chip swimlane
```

**Lanes are the real OS `pid` / `tid`** — no synthetic numbering. The roles already map
1:1 onto real threads, so real ids are sufficient *and* strictly more useful:

- `Scheduler` owns a dedicated `sched_thread_`
- `WorkerThread` is documented as *"one worker, one std::thread"*
- `Orchestrator` has no thread of its own — it runs on the caller (Python facade) thread
- each chip child is a real `fork()`, so it already has its own pid

Real ids additionally let a busy lane be taken straight to `perf top -t <tid>`,
`gdb -p <pid>`, or `/proc`, and need no mapping table that can drift. The only thing to add
is `process_name` / `thread_name` metadata so Perfetto shows names instead of bare numbers —
a labelling concern, not an identity one.

**Spans** — one per real decision point (deliberately *not* the internal lane CAS or every
`poll_progress` iteration; those are too hot to instrument):

| span | site |
| --- | --- |
| `l3.graph_build` | Python `Worker._submit_l3_locked`, around the serialized graph callback |
| `l3.submit` | `Orchestrator::submit_next_level`, after task-slot allocation |
| `l3.dispatch` | `WorkerThread::enqueue_dispatch`, after successful publication |
| `l3.frame_submit` | `LocalMailboxEndpoint::submit_progress` |
| `l3.activate` | `activate_progress` |
| `l3.complete` | `finish_progress_dispatch` |

**Scheduler phases** (optional second tier — the loop is hot enough that instrumenting
every iteration would perturb what it measures). `Scheduler::run()` has the same shape as
the AICPU loop that chip swimlane already profiles:

```
loop {
    completion_cv_.wait(...)     // sched.wait
    Phase 1: drain completions   // sched.drain
    Phase 2: dispatch_ready()    // sched.dispatch
}
```

That split is the direct answer to "is the host starved, or slow to dispatch?".

**Three cases the design has to serve:**

- **L3/L2 run interleaving** — falls out of real ids for free: parent and child are
  different pids on a shared `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`, so overlapping runs are visibly
  overlapping. Requires only that the child actually emits spans.
- **Detail inside one `worker.run`** — spans on the same `(pid, tid)` nest by `ts`/`dur`
  containment automatically. **But `l3.graph_build` (facade thread) and `l3.dispatch`
  (`WorkerThread`) are on different tids and will not nest** — that pair needs an explicit
  Chrome flow event (`ph:"s"`/`ph:"f"`). This is the real reason flow arrows are needed,
  not aesthetics.
- **Device timing info printed by the host** — already emitted: the host prints device-domain
  phases after readback as `clk=dev` spans under `simpler_run.runner_run.device_wall`
  (`strace_timing.py` derives its Device/Orch/Sched/Effective columns from exactly these).
  Draw them on a separate device sub-track, **keeping the `clk=dev` tag and doing no
  alignment**. Rendering them alongside is not the same as placing them on the host axis —
  the latter needs a measured clock anchor and is explicitly out of scope. Merging them into
  the host axis would *look* aligned while being wrong, which is worse than keeping them apart.

**Gating:** reuse the existing `SIMPLER_HOST_STRACE` compile-time gate. **No new environment
variable or macro.** When off, C++ markers and the logger lookup compile out, Python takes
its direct-call path, and throughput must not regress.

### Alternatives Considered

- **Extend `--trace-out` instead of adding a mode** — rejected: its per-invocation grouping
  is the right shape for a call-tree view and may have consumers; the two answer different
  questions and should coexist.
- **Synthesize role-based lane ids** (`tid 0=facade, 1=orch, 2=sched, 10+=chip`) — rejected
  after checking the code: the roles already correspond 1:1 to real threads, so synthetic ids
  would re-number real ones with zero added information while losing `perf`/`gdb`/`/proc`
  correlation and adding a mapping table that can drift.
- **Go straight to a unified L4→L3→L2→L0 trace** (shared pid numbering, host/device clock
  alignment, cross-level flow arrows) — deferred. The dominant use case is looking at one
  level at a time, and bundling the independent, immediately useful piece (host has no
  timeline at all) with the two hard ones (clock calibration, hierarchy folding) would block
  the former on the latter.

### Additional Context

Sub-issue of #995 (DFX capability tracking), alongside the two shipping swimlanes:

- `docs/dfx/chip-swimlane-profiling.md` — L2
- `docs/dfx/core-swimlane-profiling.md` — L0

Two forward-compatibility constraints, so a future unified view does not require redoing
this work — **neither adds effort now**:

1. Carry the run/task/endpoint keys as span attributes (they are needed for joins anyway).
2. Keep device timestamps tagged `clk=dev` with **no fake alignment** — applying a guessed
   offset now would make every historical trace untrustworthy later.

Landing constraints worth stating up front:

- **One sink.** All spans cross the `_task_interface` extension boundary; add a non-variadic
  host-span emit C entry point to the existing process-global `libsimpler_log.so`. Do not
  compile a private logger into `_task_interface` and do not introduce a second Python
  grammar.
- **Preload before `fork()`.** The child must inherit an already-loaded logger. Getting the
  order wrong shows up as *"the child's spans are all missing"* rather than as an error.
- **Unsupported topologies disable quietly.** A SUB-only L3, an L4+ `add_worker`, or a
  remote-only parent has no `_l3_bins` logger path; the bridge stays off and initialization
  must still succeed.

## #1710 Code health: three scheduler trees pay one deinit timeout per dead core on fatal shutdown

- State: open
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1710
- Created: 2026-08-06T05:49:30Z
- Updated: 2026-08-06T05:49:30Z
- Closed: 

### Body

## Description

`emergency_shutdown` has two shapes in the tree after #1664.

The a2a3 `tensormap_and_ringbuffer` scheduler broadcasts the AICore exit signal to every handshake'd core first, then joins them against a **single shared deadline**:

```cpp
for (...) platform_signal_aicore_exit(reg_addr);          // broadcast
const uint64_t exit_deadline = platform_aicore_exit_deadline();
for (...) platform_finish_aicore_exit(reg_addr, exit_deadline);   // join, one deadline
```

The other three trees still run the serial `platform_deinit_aicore_regs` loop — signal, wait, quiesce, next core.

**These three are not defective.** They never lost the acknowledgement wait, so every core is still quiesced and the card stays usable for the next process. The difference is cost, and it is worth measuring rather than assuming:

- The serial shape pays **one full deinit timeout per unresponsive core**. Onboard that is `inner_get_deinit_timeout_ticks() == PLATFORM_PROF_SYS_CNT_FREQ`, i.e. 1 s per core.
- A fatal run where every core is dead is the common case, not the rare one — the AICore fault is what triggered the shutdown.
- So an N-core fatal shutdown burns ~N seconds inside the AICPU op. That is the same order as the STARS op-execute timeout that kills `aicpu-sd`, which means a slow fatal teardown can be reaped as a hang and masked as a different failure.
- The shared-deadline shape caps the whole group at one timeout regardless of core count. On the sim variants the per-core timeout is 10 s, so the gap is larger there.

The three trees also lack the `publish_fatal_shutdown` fence, which keeps a healthy per-thread `shutdown()` from racing the emergency broadcast over the same cores.

This was deliberately left out of #1664's scope: it would mean changing three schedulers that work correctly today, and a5 hardware was not available to validate them. @ChaoZheng109 reviewed that scoping and agreed, asking that the N-second cost be measured before deciding whether to touch these trees.

## Location

- `src/a2a3/runtime/host_build_graph/runtime/scheduler/scheduler_cold_path.cpp`
- `src/a5/runtime/host_build_graph/runtime/scheduler/scheduler_cold_path.cpp`
- `src/a5/runtime/tensormap_and_ringbuffer/runtime/scheduler/scheduler_cold_path.cpp`
- `src/a5/platform/shared/aicpu/platform_regs.cpp` (would need `platform_signal_aicore_exit` / `platform_finish_aicore_exit`)

Reference implementation: `src/a2a3/runtime/tensormap_and_ringbuffer/runtime/scheduler/scheduler_cold_path.cpp::signal_emergency_shutdown`, and the shared-deadline helpers in `src/a2a3/platform/shared/aicpu/platform_regs.cpp`.

## Proposed Fix

1. **Measure first.** Instrument or time a fatal shutdown on each affected runtime with every core dead, and record the wall time inside the AICPU op against that platform's op-execute timeout. If the N-second cost does not approach the timeout, closing this as won't-fix is a legitimate outcome.
2. If it does, port the a2a3/tmr shape: add `platform_signal_aicore_exit` / `platform_finish_aicore_exit(reg_addr, deadline)` plus `platform_aicore_exit_deadline()` to a5's `platform_regs`, then broadcast-then-join with one shared deadline in each scheduler.
3. Add the `publish_fatal_shutdown` fence alongside, so `shutdown()` no-ops once fatal shutdown starts.
4. Land per tree with hardware validation for that arch, not as one sweep — a5 changes need a5 silicon.

## #1712 [Feature] hbg: Support dynamic boundary scalars in Graph Execution (Step 2)

- State: closed
- URL: https://github.com/hw-native-sys/simpler/issues/1712
- Created: 2026-08-06T07:04:52Z
- Updated: 2026-08-10T02:57:04Z
- Closed: 2026-08-10T02:57:04Z

### Body

## Summary

Graph Execution (a2a3 `host_build_graph`) cannot cache a Graph whose boundary `CoreTaskArgs` carries any scalar. `rt_graph_args_cacheable` (`graph_cache.h`) rejects `scalar_count() != 0`, so such a call falls back to the ordinary submit path. Only scalars that are fixed literals inside the Graph function (baked into the Definition) are cacheable.

## Motivation / Use Case

Real Qwen decode passes per-layer / per-token scalars (`layer_id`, `token_position`) through the boundary. Because any boundary scalar makes the Graph uncacheable, **every decode layer falls back to ordinary submission** — the Graph cache never hits in the exact per-token decode workload the feature is motivated by. Without dynamic boundary scalars, Graph Execution does not apply to real decode.

## Proposed API / Behavior

Per the `GRAPH_EXECUTION.md` roadmap (Step 2): let a boundary execution scalar carry its boundary source index and patch it at expansion exactly like a boundary tensor address. The cache key stays unchanged (execution scalar values were never part of identity); construction parameters stay on the config channel. Provenance must be seeded explicitly at the snapshot point so a scalar adjusted through the mutable accessor is not silently overwritten on replay (the trap noted in the roadmap).

## Additional Context

- Rejection site: `src/a2a3/runtime/host_build_graph/runtime/graph_cache.h` — `rt_graph_args_cacheable` (`scalar_count() != 0` -> false).
- Roadmap: `src/a2a3/runtime/host_build_graph/docs/GRAPH_EXECUTION.md` (dynamic execution scalars deferred to Step 2).
- Sub-issue of #1706.
